hero.headline: Jensen Beach Park cafe and restrooms rebuild expected by late 2027
hero.teaser: Beachgoers at Jensen Beach Park have been left with only one small restroom facility since the park's cafe and restrooms burned down on New Year's Eve in December 2024.
hero.body:
The restrooms and concession building at Jensen Beach Park remain an empty plot of land more than 18 months after a fire destroyed them on New Year's Eve in December 2024. Kevin Abbate, the Parks and Recreation director, said the permitting process takes time because the county is sitting on a protected dune and must go through the Department of Environmental Protection. The design for the new 9,000 square foot Sea Turtle Beach Cafe is 80 percent complete. The facility will be about 15 feet in elevation with 100 seats and 33 at the bar.

Final funding is expected to be approved in September, with construction starting in early 2027 and completion targeted for late 2027, just in time for the winter season. Abbate said the county wants to design the project properly so there will be fewer issues and a smoother process when construction is complete. The permit is currently in process with the Department of Environmental Protection.

Beachgoer Gonda Ghebert, who contacted local media, said beachgoers are left with only one very small restroom facility to serve the entire beach and feels it has become increasingly unreasonable during weekends, holidays, and peak tourist season. The county does not have plans for additional temporary restrooms or facilities. Other frequent beachgoers say they miss the cafe as well. Julie Goings said the facility had nice, clean showers and it was convenient being able to get a snack or drink. Sam Elliott said the only thing really missing is concessions and food availability.

Goings said she is hoping for the bathrooms to be up and running and said it would be nice to have another convenient spot. Elliott said he is hoping the project moves real fast. Abbate emphasized that designing the cafe properly will result in a smoother process and fewer issues once construction is complete.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man, 66, dies after shooting on Essex Drive in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: A 66-year-old Fort Pierce man died Tuesday after being shot at a home in the 2700 block of Essex Drive, according to the St.
cards.body:
A 66-year-old Fort Pierce man died Tuesday after being shot at a home in the 2700 block of Essex Drive, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. The victim was identified as Andre Leonard Barnes.

Deputies responded around 3:30 p.m. to the home after receiving reports of a person with a gunshot wound. When deputies arrived, they learned an adult man had shot another adult man with a rifle. Deputies took the suspect into custody and began providing emergency medical care to Barnes until St. Lucie County Fire District personnel arrived. Barnes was then taken to a local hospital, where he died. Detectives with the sheriff's office's Criminal Investigations Division are continuing to process evidence, conduct interviews, and work to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. The suspect remains in custody. Investigators say there is no threat to the public.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce to overhaul waterfront development process after multiple lawsuits
cards.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously Monday night to reject a settlement offer from plaintiff Kevin Keene, who is suing the city over its handling of the historic Little Jim's Bait & Tackle restaurant. The rejection means more taxpayer dollars will likely go toward defending the case. City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the settlement was not practical, particularly a provision that would have required taxpayers to vote on future waterfront land decisions. Broderick also said he feels the lawsuit does not have any merit. Keene told WPTV he will continue the litigation and continue the fight.

The Little Jim Bait & Tackle case is at least the fourth waterfront property dispute WPTV has reported on, and the second to result in a lawsuit. In 2023, the developer of King's Landing threatened legal action after claiming the city sold him buildable land filled with old power plant concrete. In 2024, the developer of Fisherman's Wharf, Chris Shelli, filed suit against the city after state records showed the city promised property it didn't own. In 2025, Little Jim's land lease expired and the city sought bids to take over the property. Amid public outcry, the city abruptly canceled the process, prompting Keene's lawsuit and leaving at least two developers frustrated. This year, the city became responsible for nearly $200,000 in unpaid rent tied to Crabby's Waterfront Restaurant.

Broderick acknowledged problems with how the city has managed waterfront properties. He said the handling of city-owned real estate that the city leases out to tenants is not being managed, calling it an issue he takes very seriously. Broderick said fixing the problem will take a top down, bottom up approach to look at the entirety of the portfolio of the city of Fort Pierce and fix this one asset at a time. The city is creating a new real estate management position to track leases, rent payments, and waterfront properties with the goal of preventing these problems from happening again.

Both sides say they are open to negotiating. Keene says he wants transparency, not money, and is willing to revise his offer. Broderick says he will consider any feasible settlement that keeps the case out of court. Broderick told WPTV he will not rest until he gets to the bottom of this issue, saying it will be categorized and spreadsheeted.

cards.headline: 66-year-old Fort Pierce man killed in Essex Drive shooting, suspect in custody
cards.teaser: Andre Leonard Barnes, 66, of Fort Pierce died Tuesday after being shot with a rifle at a home in the 2700 block of Essex Drive in St.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has identified the victim in Tuesday afternoon's shooting on Essex Drive as Andre Leonard Barnes, 66, of Fort Pierce. Deputies responded around 3:30 p.m. to a home in the 2700 block of Essex Drive after receiving reports of a person with a gunshot wound. When deputies arrived, they learned an adult man had shot another adult man with a rifle.

Deputies took the suspect into custody and began providing emergency medical care to Barnes until St. Lucie County Fire District personnel arrived. Barnes was then taken to a local hospital, where he died. Detectives with the sheriff's office's Criminal Investigations Division are continuing to process evidence, conduct interviews, and work to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. The suspect remains in custody. Investigators say there is no threat to the public.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man dies days after double shooting on South 14th Street
cards.teaser: A 28-year-old man died Tuesday from gunshot wounds sustained in an early Sunday morning shooting in Fort Pierce that also injured a woman.
cards.body:
The shooting happened early Sunday morning at about 3:43 a.m. in the 300 block of South 14th Street. Officers arrived at the scene and found two people with apparent gunshot wounds. A 28-year-old man sustained multiple gunshot wounds and was taken to a local hospital but died from his injuries on Tuesday. Officers also found a 28-year-old woman with injuries to her hand from the shooting, but her injuries were described as not life-threatening.

Police said a preliminary investigation indicated that the victims had been involved in an earlier altercation in the 5800 block of Okeechobee Road before returning to their residence. As they arrived home, police said a man believed to be involved in the previous altercation approached and opened fire before fleeing the area. Police said this investigation remains active and ongoing. The names of the victims have not been released. Anyone with information in the case is encouraged to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

cards.headline: Lionel Messi leads Argentina to 3-2 comeback victory over Egypt in World Cup round of 16
cards.body:
Lionel Messi scored his eighth goal of the 2026 World Cup and led Argentina to a 3-2 comeback victory over Egypt on Tuesday despite trailing by two goals with only 11 minutes of regulation time remaining. The defending champions will next face either Switzerland or Colombia in the quarterfinals on Saturday in Kansas City, Missouri. The 39-year-old was in tears after the final whistle as Argentina completed one of the great World Cup comebacks.

Messi scored his record-extending 21st goal at the World Cup in the 83rd minute to level the score at 2-2. Enzo Fernandez scored the winning goal in stoppage time to complete the rally, while Cristian Romero started the comeback in the 79th minute. Argentina had trailed 2-0 on goals from Yasser Ibrahim and Mostafa Zico. Ibrahim gave Egypt a surprising lead in the 15th minute when he got ahead of Lisandro Martinez to meet Marwan Attia's cross and head the ball into the bottom corner. Zico's goal came in the 67th minute from a sweeping break. Egypt thought it had scored earlier in the second half when Zico finished off an attack, but the goal was disallowed after video review confirmed a foul earlier in the move. "This is a phenomenal group that never gives up," Fernandez said. "Four years have passed since Qatar, and we've come to enjoy another World Cup, and we want to win it again. That's what we're aiming for."

Messi missed a penalty kick in the first half when his shot was saved by Egypt goalkeeper Mostafa Shobeir after Haissem Hassan tripped Nicolas Tagliafico in the box. He later hit the post when the score was 1-0. Shobeir also pulled off a great save to stop Julian Alvarez from close range. Despite being the all-time leading scorer at the World Cup, Messi has now missed four of eight penalty kicks at the tournament. He also failed from the spot against Austria in the group stage.

Argentina is bidding to become the first team to win back-to-back World Cup titles since Brazil did so in 1958 and 1962. For much of the game, it looked like it would be a painful exit for Messi in what might be the last of his six World Cups. Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni said he was emotional about the group of players after the match. "I'm so emotional," Scaloni said. "What a group of players, brother."

cards.headline: Leon County judge sets July hearing on GOP governor candidate's ballot eligibility
cards.body:
A Leon County judge has scheduled a two-day hearing for July 21 and 22 to determine whether Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback meets Florida's seven-year residency requirement and can remain on the August 18 primary ballot. Judge David Frank warned attorneys during a Tuesday scheduling hearing of an extreme shortage of time with the primary approaching and indicated it is likely already too late to stop ballots from being printed.

Lieutenant Governor Jay Collins filed the lawsuit challenging Fishback's eligibility, citing records tied to Fishback's voter registration and residency in Washington, D.C. Judge Frank explained that if Fishback is disqualified, the remedy would be an injunction to the Department of State instructing county supervisors of elections not to count votes for Fishback and to post notices. Fishback's attorney, former state representative Anthony Sabatini, told the court that the case turns on more than paperwork and that Fishback's intent will be central to determining residency. Sabatini said the defense wants time to present witnesses and documents.

The legal battle erupted publicly during last week's GOP primary debate, which featured Fishback, Collins and former House Speaker Paul Renner. Frontrunner Byron Donalds skipped the event but still loomed large over the debate, with his rivals repeatedly invoking him and his position in the race. Fishback pressed Collins directly over the lawsuit, getting the lieutenant governor to note his Florida roots. He told Collins to drop the lawsuit, declaring "Case closed." He later accused Collins of trying to steal the election with Byron Donalds. Collins responded that the challenge belongs in court, saying "That is a matter for the court. I actually respect the judicial system."

For now, Fishback remains on the ballot, but the case adds uncertainty to the primary calendar at a time when election officials are already preparing ballots and candidates are running out of time to shift the race. Witness and exhibit lists are due five days before the July 21 hearing. Even if Fishback is removed, the broader GOP contest may still revolve around Donalds, who has maintained a commanding position in the primary through polling, fundraising and endorsements. Axios reported Tuesday that Donalds continues to tower over the field as the August 18 primary approaches.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County pancreatic cancer patient approved for experimental treatment
cards.teaser: Russell Reed, 64, of St. Lucie County, spent 62 days waiting to learn whether he would be approved to receive daraxonrasib, an experimental drug his oncologist believed could help.
cards.body:
Reed's oncologist submitted a request through the FDA's Expanded Access Program, which can allow patients with serious or life-threatening illnesses to receive treatments outside of clinical trials when other options are limited. Daraxonrasib, also known as RMC-6236, is an investigational once-daily oral pill developed by Revolution Medicines. The drug targets mutated KRAS proteins, which drive more than 90 percent of pancreatic cancers. Reed spent 62 days waiting to learn whether he would be approved to receive the experimental drug after traditional treatments were no longer effective.

Just two days after sharing their story with WPTV, Reed learned he had been approved to receive the treatment. The drug is now in his hands, and his family says he is already feeling better and optimistic about what comes next. Reed said research and clinical trial results gave him hope that daraxonrasib could help slow the progression of his disease. While daraxonrasib is not considered a cure for pancreatic cancer, the Reeds say the approval represents something they have been fighting for all along: more time together. Marnie Reed said the fight was never just about accessing a drug but about more family trips, more memories and more moments together.

hero.headline: Jensen Beach Park restroom and concession rebuild not expected until late 2027
hero.teaser: Beachgoers at Jensen Beach Park are waiting for the rebuild of the park's restrooms and concession building destroyed in a New Year's Eve fire in December 2024.
hero.body:
The site of Jensen Beach Park's former restroom and concession building is currently an empty plot of land, more than a year after a fire destroyed the facility on New Year's Eve in December 2024. Beachgoer Gonda Ghebert wrote to WPTV that beachgoers are left with only one very small restroom facility to serve the entire beach, which has become increasingly unreasonable during weekends, holidays, and peak tourist season. Those who frequent the beach say they also miss the cafe that previously offered showers, snacks, and drinks. "The reason I went there was because they had a nice, clean facility, showers and it was just nice coming off the deck being able to get a snack or a drink if you like," Julie Goings said. Sam Elliott added, "That's the only thing that's really missing is concessions and food availability."

Kevin Abbate, the Parks and Recreation director, says the permitting process takes time. "It's gotta go through the Department of Environmental Protection. We're sitting on a protected dune, so that permit is in process now," Abbate said. The design for the new 9,000 square foot Sea Turtle Beach Cafe is 80 percent complete. "It's about 15 feet in elevation, so there's a good seat for everyone, 100 seats and 33 at the bar," Abbate said.

The county says final funding is expected to be approved in September. They hope to start construction in early 2027 with a completion goal of late 2027, just in time for the winter season. The county has no plans for additional temporary restrooms or facilities. Abbate says the cafe will be worth the wait. "We want to do it right. If we design it properly, when we get through construction, we'll have fewer issues, it'll be a much smoother process," Abbate said.

Those who use the beach say they are anxiously awaiting its construction. "I'm hoping it moves real fast," Elliott said. Goings added, "I do want the bathrooms up and running and it would be nice to have another little convenient spot." The new facility is expected to provide expanded amenities compared to the original building that was lost in the fire.

cards.headline: Martin County School District to cut 16 administrative positions, save $3.9 million
cards.teaser: The Martin County School District plans to eliminate 16 administrative and district-level positions, including three assistant principal positions, as part of a reorganization for the upcoming school year.
cards.body:
The Martin County School District plans to cut district staff as part of a reorganization for the upcoming school year, saving nearly $4 million from next year's budget. Superintendent Michael Maine told WPTV Treasure Coast reporter Tyler Hatfield the plan includes eliminating 16 administrative and district-level positions, which includes three assistant principal positions and removing 42 unfilled instructional vacancies. Maine said 10 of those vacancies were held in reserve, contingent on increasing enrollment. The changes are expected to save about $3.9 million from the district's projected budget next school year. Maine said the cuts reflect how the district routinely manages staffing each year based on projected student enrollment numbers.

The Martin County School District currently enrolls 16,000 students. Maine said the goal is to protect classroom resources while streamlining operations at the district level. He described his approach as lean and mean. Not everyone is fully on board with the scope of the cuts. Abigal, whose son will be a fourth grader at Jensen Beach Elementary this fall, said she values the small class sizes and close teacher relationships the district currently offers. She said the teachers have one-to-one interactions with the kids and do different kinds of learning. Abigal said she hopes the district is careful about how deep the cuts go.

cards.headline: Vero Beach homeowner faces $9,000 annual insurance bill, may be forced to sell
cards.teaser: Kelly Hagen says her homeowners insurance has jumped from $6,000 to $9,000 annually, and without the ability to afford required impact windows, she may have to sell her Vero Beach home within months.
cards.body:
Kelly Hagen reached out to share her frustration over the relentless rise in her homeowners insurance premiums. Her home, which has three bedrooms and two baths, is about 1,500 square feet and was built in 1994. Hagen said her homeowners insurance is $9,000 a year, which equates to $750 a month on top of her mortgage payment. It went from $6,000 to the next year it was $8,000. Hagen says the financial pressure goes beyond the premium itself. Her insurance company requires impact windows, an expensive upgrade she has struggled to afford while working two jobs. She works a full-time job and then works Instacart nights and weekends.

Her situation was made worse when she was turned away for a $10,000 My Safe Florida Home grant after it took too long to find a contractor. State leaders say now is the time for homeowners to shop around, pointing to new insurers entering the market with competitive rates. One new company, Stand Insurance, is offering to help homeowners connect with affordable contractors. Stand uses AI technology to study homes and then works to pair homeowners with vendors and contractors to make repairs. When asked how much longer she can hang on with these increases in insurance, Hagen said probably just a couple more months, and then she cannot do it. She said she is going to have to leave her house and will have to try and sell her house. Leaving would be devastating.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Clerk website down for hours after third-party service issue
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Clerk and Comptroller's website was down for hours Tuesday morning, redirecting visitors to another site before coming back online around 1:30 p.m.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Clerk and Comptroller's website was down for hours Tuesday morning, redirecting visitors to another site before coming back online by about 1:30 p.m. Clerk and Comptroller Michelle Miller posted a video on social media Tuesday afternoon addressing the outage, saying the website faced a temporary redirection issue caused by a third-party service provider. Miller said at no time was personal or confidential information compromised or at risk, and that the clerk's office does not store sensitive personal information on the public-facing website.

Jose Clavijo, the agency's IT director, said they received a report just before 8 a.m. that something was wrong with the county clerk's homepage. Clavijo said as soon as he identified the problem, he told staff to turn it off and then started the investigation. The clerk's office communications team said this was not a hack because there was not any personal information compromised. The office said residents could still access information and services on the website through direct links instead of using the homepage. Clavijo said the office is working to prevent similar issues from happening again, and that as soon as they identify the exact issue, there will be a tremendous remediation.

cards.headline: Florida Department of Environmental Protection orders Fort Pierce to pay nearly $16,000 for unpermitted docks
cards.teaser: Documents obtained from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection claim Fort Pierce has been operating docks on state-owned submerged land at Little Jim's Bait & Tackle without required permits since 2021.
cards.body:
The Florida Department of Environmental Protection has ordered the city of Fort Pierce to pay nearly $16,000 by July 17. Documents WPTV obtained from the FDEP claim the city has been operating docks on state-owned submerged land at Little Jim without the required permits since 2021. The FDEP action, issued in June, comes amid a lawsuit filed by local resident Kevin Keene. Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously Monday night to reject a settlement offer in the lawsuit alleging years of waterfront mismanagement tied to historic restaurant Little Jim Bait & Tackle. Under the proposed settlement terms, Keene would have dropped the case if the city halted any new plans for Little Jim until permit issues are resolved and allowed a public vote on future waterfront land decisions.

City Commissioner Michael Broderick acknowledged the permit issue, saying his information is that the accusation is actually true, that there was an extension of the existing docks. Broderick said someone at some point extended the docks further than allowed. He plans to negotiate FDEP's fines down while the city investigates who authorized the extension. The city has filed a motion to dismiss Keene's amended complaint. The dispute traces back to last year when the Fort Pierce landmark of nearly 80 years was facing an uncertain future after its lease expired.

cards.headline: United States eliminated from World Cup after 4-1 loss to Belgium in round of 16
cards.teaser: The United States hopes for a deep World Cup run at home ended when Belgium defeated the Americans 4-1 on Monday night in Seattle.
cards.body:
The United States' hopes for a deep World Cup run at home ended when Charles De Ketelaere scored twice and assisted on another goal, helping Belgium secure a 4-1 win Monday night at Lumen Field that earned a quarterfinal berth. Belgium knocked the U.S. out in the round of 16 for the second time in 12 years and extended its unbeaten streak to 18 games. The Red Devils play 2010 champion Spain on Friday at Inglewood, California, for a semifinal berth against France or Morocco. Malik Tillman tied the score 1-1 midway through the first half with his second free kick goal of the tournament, but the Americans conceded just 61 seconds after the ensuing kickoff. Coach Mauricio Pochettino showed his frustration by kicking a rack in front of the bench, sending four water bottles flying.

American star Christian Pulisic injured his right foot when he hit a boot of Belgium captain Youri Tielemans on a 52nd-minute shot attempt and was replaced seven minutes later. Second-half substitute Romelu Lukaku added Belgium's final goal in the third minute of stoppage time before a crowd of 66,925. The Americans have dropped 11 of their last 12 games against European opponents, winning only their round of 32 match against Bosnia-Herzegovina. All six CONCACAF nations have been eliminated, with co-hosts United States, Mexico and Canada all falling in the round of 16.

cards.headline: IOC ends neutral status vetting for Russian athletes ahead of 2028 LA Olympics
cards.teaser: The International Olympic Committee advised Olympic sports bodies on Tuesday to end a three-year program vetting Russians for neutral status ahead of qualifying events for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
cards.body:
The International Olympic Committee advised Olympic sports bodies on Tuesday to end a three-year program vetting Russians for neutral status ahead of qualifying events for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The move was expected since the IOC advised two months ago that athletes from Belarus, Russia's military ally in the full military invasion of Ukraine, should be allowed again to compete with their full national identity. The IOC eased entry requirements to its own events for Russian athletes and teams while provisionally lifting its suspension since October 2023 of the Russian Olympic Committee. The terms of that suspension, imposed when the Russian Olympic body incorporated regional sports councils from occupied regions of Ukraine, no longer applied, the IOC said.

Just 32 athletes from Russia and Belarus competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics as approved neutrals and combined to win five medals. The Russian team had more than 300 athletes at the 2021 Tokyo Olympics and won 71 medals. The IOC did not yet approve letting Russian athletes and teams compete with their flag and anthem. That decision will come at an appropriate time, the committee said. The next Olympic competition is the 2026 Youth Summer Games in Dakar, Senegal opening October 31. The IOC said Russian athletes must give multiple doping controls and be part of a recognized testing program to address the lack of confidence in the global sporting community.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Mets Roll Past Jupiter 11-2 in Series Opener
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie Mets opened their road series against the Jupiter Hammerheads with an 11-2 rout Tuesday night at Roger Dean Chevrolet Stadium, leading from the first pitch to the las
cards.body:
The St. Lucie Mets opened their road series against the Jupiter Hammerheads with an 11-2 rout Tuesday night at Roger Dean Chevrolet Stadium, leading from the first pitch to the last.

Leadoff hitter Antonio Jimenez set the tone immediately, homering on the very first pitch of the game from Jupiter starter Jonas Uzcategui. Jimenez finished the night 4 for 6 with the home run, two doubles, four runs scored and two stolen bases. He came a triple short of the cycle, striking out and hitting into a fielder's choice in his final two at-bats.

Four St. Lucie pitchers held the Hammerheads to just two hits. Starter Jose Lopez, making his team debut, worked four solid innings, allowing one hit and two runs with four walks and four strikeouts. Relievers Zack Mack, Miguel Mejias and Elwis Mijares combined for five innings of one-hit relief. Mack earned the win.

The Mets built a 3-0 lead through two innings before Jupiter answered with two runs and put the tying run on third base in the fourth. Lopez escaped the jam by getting Edgardo De Leon to pop out, preserving a 3-2 lead.

St. Lucie broke the game open with four runs in the sixth. Branny De Oleo drove in a run with a single, Jimenez scored on a wild pitch, and AJ Salgado added a two-run single to push the lead to 7-2.

The Mets tacked on two unearned runs in the eighth on a Jupiter error and another run-scoring wild pitch, then closed the scoring in the ninth on a De Oleo RBI single and yet another wild pitch that brought Jimenez home.

De Oleo went 2 for 5 with three RBI and Salgado added two hits and two RBI. Julio Zayas drew four walks, while Jeremy Rodriguez walked twice and scored two runs.

The win improved St. Lucie to 8-2 at Roger Dean Chevrolet Stadium this season and marked its third straight victory over Jupiter. The Mets (4-10, 37-43) and Hammerheads (5-11, 42-40) continue their series Wednesday, with first pitch set for 6:30 p.m.

hero.headline: 18th Annual Treasure Coast Seafood Festival Returns to Vero Beach in November
hero.body:
The 18th Annual Treasure Coast Seafood Festival is scheduled to return to Vero Beach this November, according to Under The Sun Promotions, Inc. The annual event brings seafood vendors, entertainment, and activities to the Treasure Coast community.

The festival has been a recurring event in Vero Beach for nearly two decades, drawing residents and visitors to celebrate local seafood culture. Under The Sun Promotions, Inc. organizes the annual gathering, which features fresh seafood offerings and live entertainment.

Vero Beach serves as the host city for the festival, which takes place each fall. The event provides an opportunity for local vendors and restaurants to showcase their seafood dishes and culinary offerings to the community.

Specific dates, location details, and vendor information for the November festival will be announced by Under The Sun Promotions, Inc. as the event date approaches. The festival has become a regular attraction for Indian River County residents looking for family-friendly activities during the fall season.

hero.headline: Leon County judge sets July hearing on GOP governor candidate's ballot eligibility
hero.body:
A Leon County judge has scheduled a two-day hearing for July 21 and 22 to determine whether Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback meets Florida's seven-year residency requirement and can remain on the August 18 primary ballot. Judge David Frank warned attorneys during a Tuesday scheduling hearing of an extreme shortage of time with the primary approaching and indicated it is likely already too late to stop ballots from being printed.

Lieutenant Governor Jay Collins filed the lawsuit challenging Fishback's eligibility, citing records tied to Fishback's voter registration and residency in Washington, D.C. Judge Frank explained that if Fishback is disqualified, the remedy would be an injunction to the Department of State instructing county supervisors of elections not to count votes for Fishback and to post notices. Fishback's attorney, former state representative Anthony Sabatini, told the court that the case turns on more than paperwork and that Fishback's intent will be central to determining residency. Sabatini said the defense wants time to present witnesses and documents.

The legal battle erupted publicly during last week's GOP primary debate, which featured Fishback, Collins and former House Speaker Paul Renner. Frontrunner Byron Donalds skipped the event but still loomed large over the debate, with his rivals repeatedly invoking him and his position in the race. Fishback pressed Collins directly over the lawsuit, getting the lieutenant governor to note his Florida roots. He told Collins to drop the lawsuit, declaring "Case closed." He later accused Collins of trying to steal the election with Byron Donalds. Collins responded that the challenge belongs in court, saying "That is a matter for the court. I actually respect the judicial system."

For now, Fishback remains on the ballot, but the case adds uncertainty to the primary calendar at a time when election officials are already preparing ballots and candidates are running out of time to shift the race. Witness and exhibit lists are due five days before the July 21 hearing. Even if Fishback is removed, the broader GOP contest may still revolve around Donalds, who has maintained a commanding position in the primary through polling, fundraising and endorsements. Axios reported Tuesday that Donalds continues to tower over the field as the August 18 primary approaches.

cards.headline: FDA recalls frozen Publix organic blueberries in Florida, 7 other states over E. coli risk
cards.teaser: The Food and Drug Administration issued a recall for frozen Publix GreenWise Organic Blueberries shipped to stores throughout Florida and seven other states. The FDA has reported 12 confirmed cases of stomach illness linked with E. coli infections between May 11 and June 5.
cards.body:
The Food and Drug Administration has issued a recall for frozen Publix GreenWise Organic Blueberries due to possible E. coli contamination. The product, GreenWise Organic IQF Blueberries 10 oz, was shipped to Publix retail stores throughout eight states, including Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia. Consumers who purchased these blueberries are asked not to consume them and should discard them or return them to the place of purchase for a full refund.

The affected product lot is Frozen GreenWise Organic IQF Blueberries in a 10 oz package with lot code 60401 and a best by date of February 9, 2028. The FDA has reported 12 confirmed cases of consumers experiencing stomach illness between May 11, 2026 and June 5, 2026 linked with E. coli infections. Those who have consumed food contaminated with E. coli can experience severe stomach cramps, diarrhea (which may be bloody), and vomiting. Most healthy individuals can recover within a week; however, some infections can result in serious health complications. Consumers with questions or concerns about the recall can contact Info.foodsafety@comfrut.com or 336-899-5612.

cards.headline: Florida minimum wage earners need nearly 26 years to save for home down payment, study finds
cards.teaser: A new study by Smart Asset found that the median-income household earner in Florida now takes 17 months longer to save up for a down payment than in 2016. For Floridians earning minimum wage of $14 an hour, it takes nearly 26 years to save for a down payment.
cards.body:
A new study by Smart Asset found that it now takes the median-income household earner in Florida 17 months longer to save up for a down payment in 2026 than in 2016. For Floridians who earn a minimum wage of $14 an hour, it takes nearly 26 years to save up for a down payment on a home. Florida was number 25 on the list.

Residents in Idaho have been affected the most in the last 10 years, now needing 40 months longer to buy a home than in 2016. Only in three states, Louisiana, Mississippi and North Dakota, can median-income households save a down payment faster than they could in 2016. West Virginia has the nation's lowest down payment burden. A median-income household in West Virginia needs 5.5 years to save for a down payment in 2026, just three months longer than in 2016. According to the study, saving for a down payment on a minimum-wage income alone is essentially impossible in every state.

hero.headline: Jensen Beach Park restroom and concession rebuild won't finish until late 2027
hero.body:
The restrooms and concession building at Jensen Beach Park, destroyed in a fire on New Year's Eve in December 2024, remain an empty plot of land with construction not expected to begin until early 2027. Beachgoer Gonda Ghebert, who contacted the news station, complained that beachgoers are left with only one very small restroom facility to serve the entire beach, which has become increasingly unreasonable during weekends, holidays, and peak tourist season. Regular visitors say they also miss the cafe that once provided convenient access to food and drinks. Julie Goings said she chose the beach because it had nice, clean facilities and showers, and it was convenient to get a snack or drink coming off the deck. Sam Elliott noted that the only thing really missing is concessions and food availability.

Kevin Abbate, the Parks and Recreation director, explained the permitting process takes time because it must go through the Department of Environmental Protection. The park sits on a protected dune, and that permit is currently in process. The design for the new 9,000 square foot Sea Turtle Beach Cafe is 80 percent complete. The building will stand at about 15 feet in elevation with seating for 100 people and 33 at the bar.

The county says final funding is expected to be approved in September. They hope to start construction in early 2027 with a completion goal of late 2027, just in time for the winter season. The county has no plans for additional temporary restrooms or facilities during the construction period. Abbate said the cafe will be worth the wait, emphasizing the importance of doing it right. "We want to do it right. If we design it properly, when we get through construction, we'll have fewer issues, it'll be a much smoother process," Abbate said.

Beachgoers expressed their eagerness for the project to move forward. Elliott said he is hoping it moves real fast. Goings said she wants the bathrooms up and running and it would be nice to have another little convenient spot. The extended timeline means visitors will continue dealing with limited facilities for at least another year before construction even begins, with the new building not ready until late 2027 at the earliest.

cards.headline: Vision Marine Technologies plans to sell Palm City property
cards.teaser: Vision Marine Technologies announced it is selling its Palm City property after consolidating tender-rigging operations at Fort Lauderdale Marina.
cards.body:
Vision Marine Technologies completed the consolidation of its tender-rigging operations at Fort Lauderdale Marina and announced a pending sale of its Palm City property. The company is moving its Florida operations from Palm City to Fort Lauderdale.

The consolidation at Fort Lauderdale Marina is now complete. The company announced the pending sale of the Palm City property on Tuesday.

hero.headline: St. Lucie man with pancreatic cancer approved for experimental treatment after 62-day wait
hero.teaser: Russell Reed, 64, of St. Lucie County gained access to daraxonrasib, an experimental drug his oncologist believes could help slow the progression of his pancreatic cancer.
hero.body:
Russell Reed, a 64-year-old St. Lucie man battling pancreatic cancer, has gained access to an experimental treatment after a 62-day wait that left his family uncertain about his future. Reed spent those two months waiting to learn whether he would be approved to receive daraxonrasib, an experimental drug his oncologist believed could help after traditional treatments were no longer effective. The drug, also known as RMC-6236, is an investigational once-daily oral pill developed by Revolution Medicines that targets mutated KRAS proteins, which drive more than 90% of pancreatic cancers. While the treatment is not yet FDA-approved, early clinical trial results have generated optimism among some patients and physicians.

Reed's oncologist submitted a request through the FDA's Expanded Access Program, which can allow patients with serious or life-threatening illnesses to receive treatments outside of clinical trials when other options are limited. Reed said research and clinical trial results gave him hope that daraxonrasib could help slow the progression of his disease. "There's a lot of anecdotal evidence and a lot of evidence from the clinical trials that show that this is the miracle drug for pancreatic cancer," Reed said. "It is not a cure, but it will give me time." Reed explained that chemotherapy was no longer helping him at this point in his treatment.

While waiting for an answer, Reed and his wife Marnie focused on making the most of their time together. For Marnie, the fight was never just about accessing a drug. It was about more family trips, more memories and more moments together. "I need someone's attention," Marnie Reed said. "The idea of sitting here and waiting for the phone to ring is not ok with me." She emphasized the importance of being present during this difficult time. "You're still here, and if you don't pay attention, you're going to miss it," she said. "I don't want to miss a minute with him."

Just two days after sharing their story with WPTV, Reed learned he had been approved to receive the treatment. The drug is now in his hands, and his family says he is already feeling better and optimistic about what comes next. While daraxonrasib is not considered a cure for pancreatic cancer, the Reeds say the approval represents something they have been fighting for all along: more time together.

cards.headline: 28-year-old man dies after weekend shooting on South 14th Street in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: A 28-year-old man died Tuesday after being shot multiple times early Sunday morning in Fort Pierce. Police say the shooting followed an earlier altercation.
cards.body:
A 28-year-old man died Tuesday after he was shot multiple times in Fort Pierce over the weekend, according to police. The shooting happened early Sunday morning at about 3:43 a.m. in the 300 block of South 14th Street. Officers arrived at the scene and found two people with apparent gunshot wounds. The man sustained multiple gunshot wounds and was taken to a local hospital but died from his injuries on Tuesday. Officers also found a 28-year-old woman with injuries to her hand from the shooting, but her injuries were described as not life-threatening.

A preliminary investigation indicated that the victims had been involved in an earlier altercation in the 5800 block of Okeechobee Road before returning to their residence. As they arrived home, a man believed to be involved in the previous altercation approached and opened fire before fleeing the area. The investigation remains active and ongoing. The names of the victims have not been released. Anyone with information in the case is encouraged to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Clerk's website down for hours Tuesday due to third-party provider issue
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Clerk and Comptroller's website was down for hours Tuesday morning, redirecting visitors to another site before coming back online around 1:30 p.m.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Clerk and Comptroller's website was down for hours Tuesday morning, redirecting visitors to another site before coming back online by about 1:30 p.m. Clerk and Comptroller Michelle Miller posted a video on social media Tuesday afternoon addressing the outage, saying the website faced a temporary redirection issue caused by a third-party service provider. Miller assured the public that no personal or confidential information was compromised or at risk because the clerk's office does not store sensitive personal information on the public-facing website.

Jose Clavijo, the agency's IT director, said they received a report just before 8 a.m. that something was wrong with the county clerk's homepage. Clavijo said he immediately had the site turned off and started an investigation. Residents could still access information and services on the website through direct links instead of using the homepage. Clavijo said the payments page, property fraud information, and all other services remained available, with only the main page affected. The clerk's office communications team said this was not a hack because no personal information was compromised. Clavijo said the office is working to prevent similar issues and that there will be a tremendous remediation once they identify the exact issue.

cards.headline: 66-year-old Fort Pierce man killed in Essex Drive shooting, suspect in custody
cards.teaser: Andre Leonard Barnes, 66, of Fort Pierce died Tuesday after being shot with a rifle at a home in the 2700 block of Essex Drive in St.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has identified the victim in Tuesday afternoon's shooting on Essex Drive as Andre Leonard Barnes, 66, of Fort Pierce. Deputies responded around 3:30 p.m. to a home in the 2700 block of Essex Drive after receiving reports of a person with a gunshot wound. When deputies arrived, they learned an adult man had shot another adult man with a rifle.

Deputies took the suspect into custody and began providing emergency medical care to Barnes until St. Lucie County Fire District personnel arrived. Barnes was then taken to a local hospital, where he died. Detectives with the sheriff's office's Criminal Investigations Division are continuing to process evidence, conduct interviews, and work to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. The suspect remains in custody. Investigators say there is no threat to the public.
